subject: english
question:
A Form 5 student, Nicholas Yau, wrote the following note to his school's Vice-Principal to request permission to postpone a project deadline:

"hey sir, cant hand in the geog project on friday cos my group partner bailed on me last min. its not my fault tbh. can u just give us more time? thx"

(a) Identify THREE features of this note that make it inappropriate for its audience and purpose. (3 marks)
(b) Rewrite the note so that it is appropriate in tone and register, while keeping the same request and the same reason. Write 60–80 words. (3 marks)
referenceAnswer:
(a) Three of the following:
• Salutation is over-familiar ("hey sir") where a formal address ("Dear Mr …") is required for a senior member of staff.
• Abbreviated, text-message forms ("cant", "cos", "min", "u", "thx", "tbh") belong to private messaging, not to a written request to a school authority.
• The tone shifts blame onto a classmate ("my group partner bailed on me", "its not my fault") rather than taking responsibility for the request.
• "can u just give us more time" is a bare demand; a request to a superior needs a modal softener and a specific proposal.
• No new deadline is proposed, so the reader cannot act on the request.
• There is no sign-off identifying the writer, class or subject teacher.

(b) Sample rewrite (72 words):
"Dear Mr Cheung,

I am writing to ask whether my group may submit our Geography project on Tuesday 14 October instead of this Friday. One member of the group has been absent this week, and we have not been able to complete the fieldwork section on time. We would be grateful for three extra days, and we will submit the remaining sections on Friday as planned.

Yours sincerely,
Nicholas Yau (5C)"

markingScheme:
自評準則（唔係關鍵字對照，係逐項自問）：

(a) 3 分 —— 每指出一項【並說明點解對呢個讀者／目的唔恰當】得 1 分。只寫「太口語」而唔講點解，計半個點：口語本身唔係錯，錯喺對象係副校長。

(b) 3 分，三條各自問一次：
1. 語域：全篇有冇殘留縮寫、口語或表情符號？有一個都當未達。
2. 內容完整：有冇【提出具體新限期】？原文最大問題係讀者收到都唔知要批准啲乜。
3. 責任語氣：有冇將原因講成事實陳述（「一位組員本週缺席」），而唔係指責同學？

字數：60–80。超出範圍唔扣內容分，但要留意 DSE 卷二超字數會影響組織評分。
markingSchemeEn:
Self-assessment criteria (not a keyword checklist — ask yourself each question):

(a) 3 marks — 1 mark per feature identified WITH a reason why it fails this reader and purpose. Naming "too casual" without explaining why counts as half a point: informality is not wrong in itself; it is wrong when the reader is a Vice-Principal.

(b) 3 marks. Ask three questions:
1. Register: any abbreviations, slang or emoji left anywhere? Even one means not yet.
2. Completeness: did you propose a SPECIFIC new deadline? The original's worst fault is that the reader cannot act on it.
3. Ownership: is the reason stated as fact ("one member has been absent") rather than as blame?

Length 60–80 words. Going over does not cost content marks, but note that overlong answers affect the organisation mark in the real paper.
explanation:
This question trains the one thing Paper 2 markers notice first: whether you have read the AUDIENCE, not just the task.

Most candidates who lose marks here can already write correct English. What they do not do is change register when the reader changes. The same request — more time for a project — is entirely reasonable; only the packaging fails.

Notice what the rewrite does NOT do: it does not become longer, more elaborate, or full of formal-sounding vocabulary. It stays short. Formality is not the same as verbosity, and padding a request with "I would like to humbly beseech your kind consideration" is its own kind of register error.

The transferable rule: before writing a single word, decide who reads this, what they need in order to act, and what relationship the language should signal. Everything else follows from those three answers.

subject: english
question:
Read the extract below, then answer the questions.

"The library at Sha Kok Estate closed in March. The notice on the door said 'temporary'. It has now been eleven months. In that time the reading room has been used twice: once for a district consultation on refuse collection, and once, briefly, as a storage space for chairs.

Mrs Poon still walks past it on Tuesdays. She used to bring her grandson here after school, she says, because their flat has one table and her son works nights. When asked where the boy studies now, she gestures at the McDonald's across the road, and then, after a pause, adds that the staff there have never once asked him to leave."

(a) Explain how the writer uses the phrase "The notice on the door said 'temporary'" to convey a critical attitude. (3 marks)
(b) Explain the effect of the pause before Mrs Poon's final remark. (3 marks)
referenceAnswer:
(a) The criticism is carried by placement and contrast rather than by any judgemental word. The writer quotes the official word "temporary" and then, in the very next sentence, supplies the counter-evidence: "It has now been eleven months." The quotation marks distance the writer from the term, presenting it as the authority's claim rather than as fact. Nothing is asserted directly — the reader is left to conclude that "temporary" has quietly become permanent, and a conclusion the reader reaches unaided is harder to dismiss than an accusation.

(b) The pause marks the moment Mrs Poon recognises what her own gesture has admitted. Pointing at the McDonald's is offered as a simple answer; the hesitation shows her registering that it is also an indictment. Her added remark — that the staff have never asked him to leave — is phrased as gratitude, but it quietly measures a fast-food outlet against a public library and finds the public service wanting. The pause is what turns a factual reply into a judgement, without her ever having to make one.

markingScheme:
自評準則：

(a) 3 分：
1. 有冇指出【引號】嘅作用（將「temporary」標示為官方講法而非事實）？
2. 有冇引用緊接嘅反證（eleven months）並講出兩者嘅落差？
3. 有冇講到作者【冇直接批評】—— 即效果來自讀者自己得出結論？
第 3 點係分水嶺。只答「作者諷刺政府」而唔講佢點樣做到，屬於講咗結論冇講手法。

(b) 3 分：
1. 有冇指出停頓標誌住人物自己意識到啲乜？
2. 有冇處理「感激」同「控訴」呢個雙重性 —— 佢讚嘅係快餐店，反襯嘅係圖書館？
3. 有冇避免過度推論（例如寫成「佢好憤怒」）？文本冇支持憤怒，只支持醒覺。

常見失分位：將 (b) 答成「表達佢好無奈」。無奈係情緒標籤，唔係效果分析；題目問 effect，要講嗰個停頓對讀者理解造成咩改變。
markingSchemeEn:
Self-assessment criteria:

(a) 3 marks:
1. Did you identify what the QUOTATION MARKS do (marking "temporary" as the authority's word, not fact)?
2. Did you cite the counter-evidence that immediately follows (eleven months) and state the gap between the two?
3. Did you note that the writer makes NO direct accusation — that the effect comes from the reader reaching the conclusion unaided?
Point 3 separates a strong answer from an average one. "The writer is criticising the government" states a conclusion without showing how it is achieved.

(b) 3 marks:
1. Did you identify what the pause marks — the speaker realising something?
2. Did you handle the double edge: the remark sounds like gratitude but measures a fast-food outlet against a public library?
3. Did you avoid over-reading (e.g. "she is furious")? The text supports realisation, not anger.

Common loss: answering (b) as "it shows she feels helpless". That is an emotion label, not an effect. The question asks what the pause does to the reader's understanding.
explanation:
Paper 1 Part B rewards candidates who can say HOW a text achieves an effect, not merely WHAT the writer thinks.

Both parts here turn on the same principle: the strongest criticism in journalistic writing is usually the one the writer never states. Quotation marks, a bare factual counter-statement, an unexplained pause — these hand the judgement to the reader, who then owns it.

When a question asks about "attitude" or "effect", resist the urge to name an emotion and stop. Name the DEVICE, quote it, then say what it makes the reader do. Three moves, every time.

One warning about over-reading. Part (b) tempts you to invent a feeling the text does not support — anger, bitterness, despair. The passage gives you a pause and one added sentence. Build only what those two things can carry. Inventing emotion is the single most common way candidates lose marks on inference questions, and it is entirely avoidable.

subject: english
question:
DATA FILE

Source A — Extract from a school survey (312 respondents, Forms 4–6):
• 68% said they "often" or "always" study with background music.
• Of those, 71% chose instrumental or lo-fi tracks; 29% chose songs with lyrics.
• 54% of all respondents said they would find a silent study room "stressful".

Source B — Note from the school librarian:
"We trialled a silent-only rule last term. Usage dropped from about 40 students a day to 12. The ones who stopped coming were mostly Form 4. Several told me they went to fast-food outlets instead, which are noisier, not quieter — so I do not think noise was the real issue. I suspect the rule made the library feel like an exam hall."

Source C — Student comment collected by the Student Union:
"I can concentrate with music. What I cannot do is concentrate while worrying that someone will tap me on the shoulder."

TASK
You are the Chairperson of the Student Union. Write a proposal (180–220 words) to the Principal recommending ONE change to the library's rules. Your proposal must:
• state the recommendation clearly;
• use evidence from at least TWO of the sources;
• acknowledge one reasonable objection and respond to it.
referenceAnswer:
Sample response (205 words):

"Dear Dr Lam,

Proposal: a designated 'headphones permitted' zone in the library

The Student Union recommends that the eastern half of the reading room be designated a headphones-permitted zone, with the western half remaining silent.

Our survey of 312 students found that 68% study with background music, and that 54% would find a fully silent room stressful. This is not a marginal preference. The librarian's own trial supports the same conclusion from a different direction: when a silent-only rule was introduced, daily usage fell from about 40 students to 12, and those who left went to noisier fast-food outlets rather than quieter ones. As she notes, noise was evidently not the deciding factor; the atmosphere was.

One reasonable objection is that a divided room is harder to supervise and may erode the silent area over time. We propose two safeguards: a clear floor marking rather than a movable sign, and a one-term review using the same daily-usage count the librarian already keeps, so the decision can be reversed on evidence rather than impression.

We believe this change addresses the real barrier identified in the trial — students avoiding a space that felt like an examination hall — without removing the silent option for those who need it.

Yours sincerely,
Chairperson, Student Union"

markingScheme:
自評準則（10 分，四條軸各自問一次）：

1. 建議清晰（2 分）：讀者讀完第一段，知唔知道要批准啲乜？寫「改善圖書館氣氛」唔算建議，寫「東半邊劃為可戴耳機區」先算。

2. 引用資料（3 分）：
   · 有冇用到至少兩個來源？
   · 引用嘅係【具體數字或事實】（68%、40→12），定係含糊轉述（「好多人話」）？
   · 有冇解釋數據點解支持你個建議 —— 唔係貼咗數字就當論證。

3. 處理反對（3 分）：
   · 你提出嗰個反對，係咪一個【真係合理】嘅反對？寫一個明顯站唔住嘅反對嚟打，係稻草人。
   · 你嘅回應有冇提出可操作嘅補救，定係淨係話「應該唔會發生」？

4. 語域同格式（2 分）：正式稱謂、有標題、有署名；全篇冇口語同縮寫。

⚠️ 呢份準則係【俾你自己對照】嘅。DSE 卷三由真人評卷，冇任何機器可以按關鍵字判你對錯，本平台亦永遠唔會咁做。

常見失分位：Source C（學生留言）最易被當成裝飾。佢其實提供咗最關鍵嘅一句 —— 問題唔係聲音，係被監視嘅焦慮。用得到呢一點，成篇論證就唔同層次。
markingSchemeEn:
Self-assessment criteria (10 marks, four axes — ask yourself each):

1. Clear recommendation (2 marks): after the first paragraph, does the reader know exactly what they are being asked to approve? "Improve the library atmosphere" is not a recommendation; "designate the eastern half as a headphones-permitted zone" is.

2. Use of sources (3 marks):
   · Did you draw on at least TWO sources?
   · Did you cite SPECIFIC figures or facts (68%, 40 → 12) rather than vague paraphrase ("many people said")?
   · Did you explain why the evidence supports your recommendation? Quoting a number is not the same as arguing from it.

3. Handling the objection (3 marks):
   · Is the objection you raised one a reasonable person would actually raise? Attacking an obviously weak objection is a straw man.
   · Does your response offer a workable safeguard, or does it merely assert that the problem will not arise?

4. Register and format (2 marks): formal salutation, a heading, a sign-off; no colloquialisms or abbreviations anywhere.

⚠️ These criteria are for YOUR OWN comparison. Paper 3 is marked by a human examiner; no machine can grade this by keyword, and this platform will never attempt to.

Common loss: Source C is easily treated as decoration. It in fact supplies the sharpest point in the file — the barrier is not noise but the anxiety of being watched. An answer that uses it argues on a different level from one that does not.
explanation:
Paper 3 is not a writing test with data attached. It is a test of whether you can turn evidence into an argument.

The trap built into this data file is that Sources A and B appear to say the same thing, and Source C looks like a throwaway quotation. In fact the three do different jobs: A establishes scale, B supplies a natural experiment with a counter-intuitive result, and C names the mechanism. A candidate who only stacks A and B has evidence but no explanation. A candidate who reaches C can say WHY the silent rule failed — and a proposal that identifies a cause is far more persuasive than one that only reports a correlation.

Note also what the model response does with the objection. Weak candidates raise an objection they can easily dismiss. Strong candidates raise the one the reader is already thinking of — here, that a divided room will drift — and then answer it with something concrete and reversible. Offering a review mechanism signals that you are arguing in good faith rather than lobbying.

The underlying skill transfers well beyond this paper: evidence tells you what happened; only a mechanism tells you what to do about it.
